Lane's catalogue raisonné identifies the foreground of ⟦0⟧Ten Pound Island, Gloucester⟦1⟧ as George Rogers's wharf on Fort Point, with the island at center and Eastern Point beyond; Erik Ronnberg aligned the viewpoint on the 1865 Harbor Commissioners' chart.⟦2⟧ For ⟦3⟧Ship in Fog⟦4⟧ the catalogue puts Lane in the channel “just off Fort Point.”⟦5⟧ The 1847 Thyssen picture was taken from a little higher and farther back, near Duncan's Point.
The catalogue calls the light of ⟦0⟧Ten Pound Island⟦1⟧ “the hazy light of a late summer afternoon,” in apricot hues.⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧Ship in Fog⟦4⟧ is early morning, the summer sea fog burning off in stages.
The island and harbor mouth are unchanged in outline, but Fort Point's 1850s wharves are gone, and the tower Lane painted (1821) was replaced in 1881.
We could not confirm public shore access on Fort Point itself. Ten Pound Island is also visible across the water from a public way on Rocky Neck.
For the Lane effect, go in late August, about two hours before sunset; for the fog picture, a still June or July morning.

In summer 1880 Homer boarded on Ten Pound Island with the lighthouse keeper, Oliver Merrill.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ Princeton places ⟦2⟧Eastern Point Light⟦3⟧ in the series “painted by Homer on Ten Pound Island.”⟦4⟧ Where on the island he sat is not recorded; the line on the map runs from the island's light to Eastern Point Light, almost due south.

Eastern Point Light⟦0⟧ is a moonlit night: rapid blue washes for the sky, the full moon “scraped out,” the water dappled by gouging with the brush end.⟦1⟧ Most of the series are sunsets over the western shore;⟦2⟧ in early August the sun sets in the west-northwest, to the painter's right when facing the harbor mouth.
The island is owned by the City of Gloucester, which keeps walking paths to the light; private boaters may land, but there is no landing facility. The tower itself is Coast Guard property and closed.
Without a boat, paint the island and Homer's sunsets from the Rocky Neck public way, looking west across the harbor.
Homer's 1880 method, per the MFA: let paint soak into the paper, blot it out, then lay on thick opaque dashes.
Site 3 of 9 · Willard Metcalf and Childe Hassam

Banner Hill is the ridge above Smith Cove, from which “many of the most notable American impressionist landscapes of Gloucester were painted.”⟦0⟧ Metcalf's ⟦1⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦2⟧ was “painted from Banner Hill looking westward”; Hassam's 1899 view was taken from the same hill, “a little farther to the left” than Duveneck's.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ The marker is the hill's road (OpenStreetMap); the exact spots are not recorded.

Metcalf painted “with the morning sun at the artist's back,” so the town across the harbor is lit full-face.⟦0⟧ At 9 a.m. in early August the sun stands in the east, about 36° up, behind and to the right of a painter facing downtown.
The Banner Hill vantage is now private property and not open to the public; the view can be seen from the road.
Go in the morning. In the afternoon the town is backlit and the harbor turns to glare.
Rocky Neck's Art Trail marks this and other historic painting sites.

Lane's source drawing is inscribed “Brace's Rock, Eastern Point / F.H. Lane del. / Aug. 1863” and lists five buyers for paintings made from it. The catalogue says he drew from “the coast just north of the cove,” not the beach.⟦0⟧ The marker is the nearest shore point north of the cove (MassGIS); the exact spot is not recorded. Duveneck painted the same rock about 1893.⟦1⟧ From the marker the rock lies south-southeast; because the Terra Foundation describes Lane's view as looking east across the cove, he may have stood farther west along the shore.

The Terra Foundation describes the view as looking east across the cove, “the unseen sun in the west” tinting the far rocks pink while the foreground lies in shadow: late afternoon.⟦0⟧ One version shows autumn foliage, so Lane varied the season.
In Lane's day the cove was part of the private Niles Farm, with Niles Pond between it and the harbor.⟦0⟧ We could not verify public shore access today.
Go late in the afternoon with the sun behind you, and watch the far rocks turn warm in the last hour.
Lane worked from a measured drawing, then painted several near-identical canvases from it. Make the drawing on site and the painting at home.

Lane “drew the rock from the shore looking to the south” in 1861, on a drawing gridded for transfer; the boat drifts in the cove just north of the rock. The catalogue includes a viewpoint chart.⟦0⟧ The marker is the nearest shore point north of the cove (MassGIS).

A newspaper in 1862 called it “a sunset scene”: the sky moves from purple at upper left to coppery yellow at right, the light of early twilight.⟦0⟧ Facing south, the setting sun is off to the right (west), which is where Lane put his brightest sky.
The rock lies a few hundred feet offshore and can be reached over the rocks at low tide; at high tide it is an island.⟦0⟧ Mind the tide: the harbor range averages nearly 9 feet.
OpenStreetMap shows a Normans Woe Wildlife Sanctuary along this shore; we did not verify its access rules.
Go for the last half hour before sunset, and keep the sky warm on the right and cool at upper left, as Lane did.

The back of the canvas reads “View of Coffin's Beach, from the rocks at the Loaf, after a sketch taken, August, 1862.” Ronnberg plotted the viewpoint, and MFA staff concluded Lane used a camera lucida, then widened the scene in the painting.

Dawn: an 1862 notice says the sun is just rising behind the hills, in pink-to-blue light.⟦0⟧ At sunrise in early August the sun comes up in the east-northeast, nearly straight down the line of view, so the scene is backlit.
The Two Penny Loaf is mapped as a nature reserve (OpenStreetMap); we did not verify access to Coffin's Beach.
Be in place before sunrise (5:34 a.m. on August 1, 2027) and paint the first 20 minutes.
A camera lucida, or a phone photo traced the same way, is a fair modern stand-in for Lane's method.

A secondary source describes ⟦0⟧Horizon at Gloucester⟦1⟧ as the port's skyline “from Eastern Point.”⟦2⟧ The marker is placed at Eastern Point Light; the exact spot is not recorded. Duveneck stayed at the Harbor View Hotel in East Gloucester.

From Eastern Point the city lies almost due north, about 3.8 km away, so the sun is behind or beside the painter all day and the skyline is always lit from the front: from the east in the morning, the south at midday, the west in late afternoon.
The lighthouse is Coast Guard property and closed to the public.⟦0⟧ The Dog Bar Breakwater beside it is a 2,250-foot granite jetty: wear sturdy shoes and stay off it when waves break over the stones.
Duveneck's foreground is low-tide ledge and weed. Time a session for low water and the tide pools will give you his foreground.

The title places the picture at Lighthouse Beach beside Annisquam Light, on Wigwam Point.⟦0⟧ Jones's exact spot is not recorded, and the museum page could not be checked for it. The line on the map is a modern alternative: the light can be seen from Wingaersheek Beach across the river mouth.
No source describes the time of day. From Wingaersheek you look north at the light: morning sun is side-lit from the right, and afternoon sun comes over your left shoulder onto the tower.
The light's keeper's house is Coast Guard housing; the light can be viewed from Wingaersheek Beach.
Non-resident beach parking must be reserved in summer (Memorial Day to Labor Day).
Jones's sand and ledge change with the tide. At low water the flats here widen a great deal.

Twachtman painted ⟦0⟧Harbor View Hotel⟦1⟧ “from the end of the long pier,” the hotel's float on Wonson's Cove, looking back at the hotel with his cottage studio at far left. It was on his easel when he died there in August 1902.⟦2⟧ The hotel stood at what is now 21 Eastern Point Road.⟦3⟧ The pier's end is placed at the middle of the cove.
Not described in the sources. Facing the hotel from the cove is roughly an eastward view, so late-afternoon sun would fall full on the buildings from behind the painter.
The hotel is gone; the site is Rocky Neck Art Trail stop 15, reached on foot from Rocky Neck Avenue.
The painting is at the Nelson-Atkins Museum (33-57). Its image is not reproduced here, so look at it on the museum's page before you go.
